key_terms.meaning: D = Et³/[12(1−ν²)], where E is Young's modulus (N/m²), t is plate thickness (m) and ν is Poisson's ratio; D has units N·m.
A bent plate curves in opposite senses along two perpendicular directions, giving a saddle shape; this happens when the two bending moments have opposite sign.
A bent plate curves the same way along both directions, giving a dome shape; occurs when both bending moments have the same sign.
Plane sections normal to the mid-surface stay straight and normal after bending, and the mid-surface strains are zero in pure bending.
D∇⁴w = q + Nₓ ∂²w/∂x² + N_y ∂²w/∂y² + 2N_xy ∂²w/∂x∂y, with w the deflection (m), q the transverse pressure (N/m²) and Nₓ, N_y, N_xy the in-plane membrane forces per unit length (N/m).
In-plane force per unit length of plate edge (N/m); tensile membrane forces stiffen the plate, compressive ones soften it and can cause buckling.
A number depending on edge support and aspect ratio a/b; k = 4.0 for a simply supported plate in uniform uniaxial compression, and larger for other support and stress patterns.
σ_cr = kπ²E/[12(1−ν²)(b/t)²], with b the loaded edge width (m) and t the thickness (m); the stress at which the flat equilibrium becomes unstable.
The width w_e of buckled skin assumed to still carry compression with each stiffener; the middle of a buckled bay sheds load to the edges near the stringers.
Skin plus longitudinal stringers and transverse frames; the skin buckles first, then the panel carries load up to stringer or frame failure.
The average stress at which a short thin-walled compression element finally fails after local buckling, usually well below the material yield stress.
An empirical fit that gives crippling stress as a function of the element's b/t ratio and the material's yield and ultimate stresses for simple sections.
A semi-empirical correlation using a coefficient g and the element's flat-width-to-thickness ratio to estimate crippling stress for angles, Z- and channel sections.
The point in a cross-section through which a transverse load must act to produce no twist; in open thin-walled sections it lies away from the centroid.
Instability in which an open thin-walled column bends and twists at the same time, because the compressive load line misses the shear centre so bending and torsion couple.
A fibre-reinforced layer with three independent stiffnesses: E₁ along the fibres, E₂ across them, and shear modulus G₁₂, with ν₁₂ coupling the two directions.
The laminate stiffness set: A (extensional, N/m), B (extension–bending coupling, N) and D (bending, N·m), obtained by summing each ply's rotated stiffness through the thickness.
Every structure has frequencies ω_n (rad/s) at which it vibrates freely, and a damping ratio ζ that sets how fast free vibration dies out.

Divergence is a static aeroelastic instability where aerodynamic moment exceeds structural restoring moment; flutter is a dynamic instability where aerodynamic and elastic forces feed each other at a critical speed.
Under compression plus shear a plate buckles when (σ/σ_cr) + (τ/τ_cr)² ≈ 1 or a similar interaction curve, not when the two stresses simply add up.

takeaways: A thin plate carries load mainly by bending curvature, and its stiffness scales with t³ through the plate stiffness D.
Transverse pressure and in-plane membrane forces enter the same plate equation, so bending and stretching act together and cannot be treated separately.
A plate buckles at a stress proportional to (t/b)², so making the sheet thinner or the bay wider drops the buckling stress sharply.
After the skin buckles between stringers, the panel still carries load, but only an effective width of skin close to each stringer is counted.
Short thin-walled compression elements fail by crippling at a stress below yield, and Needham's and Gerard's correlations estimate that stress from the b/t ratio.
An open thin-walled column can fail by twisting and bending together because the load path misses the shear centre; a closed tube resists this far better.
A composite ply is orthotropic, and a laminate is analysed by summing rotated ply stiffnesses into the A, B and D matrices.
Every structure has natural frequencies and damping, and aeroelastic coupling can turn those frequencies into divergence or flutter at a critical speed.
Shear and combined compression–shear loads buckle a plate along an interaction curve, so a shear stress counts even when the direct stress is small.
bank_note: Long answers here are mostly derivations plus design judgement: state the governing equation, then the critical stress or effective width, then how the aircraft panel is actually sized.

bank.q: Define plate stiffness D and write the moment–curvature relations for a thin isotropic plate. Explain anticlastic and synclastic bending with sketches.
outline: State Kirchhoff–Love assumptions: normals stay straight and normal, no mid-surface strain.
Strain varies linearly through thickness: ε = −z ∂²w/∂x².
D = Et³/[12(1−ν²)] and explain each symbol and its unit.
Mₓ = −D(w_xx + ν w_yy), M_y = −D(w_yy + ν w_xx), M_xy = −D(1−ν)w_xy.
Anticlastic: two curvatures opposite in sign, saddle shape, one moment hogging one sagging.
Synclastic: curvatures same sign, dome shape, e.g. a spherical cap under uniform pressure.

bank.q: Explain how transverse pressure and in-plane forces combine in the governing equation of a thin plate, and state where each term comes from.
outline: Write D∇⁴w = q + Nₓ w_xx + N_y w_yy + 2N_xy w_xy.
Explain q as transverse pressure per unit area (N/m²) causing bending.
Explain Nₓ, N_y, N_xy as in-plane membrane forces per unit length (N/m).
Show that compressive membrane forces add a negative stiffness term and can drive the plate to buckling.
Note tensile membrane forces stiffen the plate (the basis of tension field action).
Give one aircraft example: fuselage skin under pressurisation plus fuselage bending.

bank.q: Describe the buckling of a thin rectangular plate under uniform uniaxial compression. Write the critical stress and explain the plate buckling coefficient k.
outline: Plate is flat and stable up to σ_cr, then deflects into a half-wave pattern in the loaded direction.
σ_cr = kπ²E/[12(1−ν²)(b/t)²]; define each symbol and unit.
k depends on edge support and aspect ratio a/b; k ≈ 4 for simply supported edges in compression.
Number of half-waves along the plate grows with aspect ratio but k stays near its minimum.
Post-buckled plate still carries load from the edges; only the middle sheds load.
Compare with column buckling: plates have much higher buckling stress for the same b/t because of two-way support.

bank.q: Explain the concept of effective sheet width in a stiffened panel after the skin buckles between stringers.
outline: Skin buckles at a low stress because b/t is large, but the panel does not fail.
Buckled skin sheds compression to the edges near the stringers.
Define effective width w_e: the width assumed to work at the full stress with each stringer.
Give a common form such as w_e ∝ t√(E/σ) and state that w_e falls as stress rises.
Total panel load = stringer load + σ × effective skin area.
Consequence for design: stringer spacing controls how much skin is useful.

bank.q: Explain why an open thin-walled column can buckle by bending and twisting together, while a closed tube rarely does. Give the role of the shear centre.
outline: Define shear centre and note it is offset from the centroid in open sections.
The compressive load acts through the centroid; the section twists about the shear centre.
Twist produces warping and longitudinal displacement, which couples with bending.
Flexural-torsional buckling load is lower than the pure Euler or pure torsion load.
Closed sections have high torsional stiffness and shear centre near the centroid, so coupling is weak.
Aircraft examples: open Z-stringers need restraint; closed spars behave better.

bank.q: A simply supported aluminium plate has E = 70 GPa, ν = 0.33, thickness 2 mm and loaded edge width 250 mm. Take k = 4.0. Calculate D and the critical buckling stress in compression.
outline: Write D = Et³/[12(1−ν²)] and substitute values with consistent units.
Show intermediate value of (1−ν²) = 0.891.
Write σ_cr = kπ²D/(b²t) and substitute b = 0.25 m, t = 0.002 m.
Comment: this is low compared to yield, so skin buckles early and effective width matters.

bank.q: Estimate the crippling stress of a thin-walled angle section in 2024 aluminium using Needham's and Gerard's methods, and compare with yield.
outline: Define flat width b, thickness t and compute b/t for each element.
State the material constants needed: yield stress and ultimate stress.
Apply Needham's empirical expression relating crippling stress to b/t and material properties.
Apply Gerard's expression σ_cr = g E (t/b)^m with the stated coefficient for the section type.
Compare the two answers and note the spread of empirical methods.
Explain why crippling stress is below yield: local buckling lets part of the section fail early.

bank.q: A thin-walled channel column of given cross-section has a stated torsional stiffness and a known offset between centroid and shear centre. Set up the calculation of its flexural-torsional buckling load.
outline: Compute section properties: area, second moments Iₓ, I_y, torsion constant J, warping constant Γ.
Locate centroid and shear centre; state the eccentricity e.
Write the Euler loads Pₓ = π²EI_y/L² and P_y = π²EIₓ/L².
Write the torsional buckling load involving GJ and EΓ.
Show that the coupled flexural-torsional load is lower than the smaller of these.
State the assumption of pinned ends and mention how end fixity changes the answer.

bank.q: For a two-ply laminate with given ply properties and fibre angles, show how the A, B and D matrices are built and state what each matrix does.
outline: State ply engineering constants E₁, E₂, ν₁₂, G₁₂ and how reduced stiffnesses Q are formed.
Rotate Q to the ply angle θ to get the transformed stiffness, with the 1/8 and 3/8 terms from cos⁴ and sin⁴.
A = Σ transformed stiffness × ply thickness; units N/m; gives in-plane load–strain relation.
B = Σ transformed stiffness × (z_k² − z_{k−1}²)/2; units N; couples extension and bending.
D = Σ transformed stiffness × (z_k³ − z_{k−1}³)/3; units N·m; gives bending stiffness.
State that a symmetric laminate has B = 0; an unsymmetric one warps when loaded.

bank.q: Using the effective width idea, estimate the load carried by a stiffened panel in compression once the skin has buckled, and compare with the unbuckled case.
outline: Give panel geometry: stringer spacing, skin thickness, number of stringers.
Compute skin buckling stress from the plate formula.
At a higher applied stress, compute effective width w_e from a stated expression.
Panel load = number of stringers × stringer area × stress + effective skin area × stress.
Compare with the load the panel would carry if the whole skin worked.
Comment on the loss of stiffness and the resulting need for closely spaced stringers.

bank.q: Explain how combined compression and shear buckle a plate. Why is the interaction a curve and not a simple sum of stresses?
outline: Shear alone buckles a plate in a diagonal wave pattern; shear buckling coefficient depends on aspect ratio.
Write the interaction relation, e.g. (σ/σ_cr) + (τ/τ_cr)² = 1, and define each term.
Explain that shear produces principal tensile and compressive stresses at 45°, so shear feeds the compressive buckling mode.
Small shear stress therefore reduces the compressive buckling load even when present alone it is safe.
Sketch the interaction curve; note it lies inside the straight-line sum.
Aircraft example: wing skin in bending plus torsion of the wing box.

bank.q: Distinguish divergence from flutter, and explain the role of natural frequency and damping in each.
outline: Define divergence: static instability where aerodynamic moment grows faster than structural restoring moment.
Divergence occurs at a speed independent of damping; derive from stiffness balance.
Define flutter: dynamic instability where two modes exchange energy with the airflow each cycle.
Flutter depends on natural frequencies of the coupled modes and on damping.
Damping raises the flutter speed only a little; matching frequencies is the real danger.
Aircraft example: control surface flutter and wing torsional divergence; mention design remedies such as mass balance and stiffness.

bank.q: Analyse why an unsymmetric composite laminate warps on curing while a symmetric one does not, and what this means for aircraft panels.
outline: Each ply shrinks differently along and across the fibres during cool-down.
In an unsymmetric layup the plies pull against each other and the B matrix is nonzero.
Coupling between extension and bending then produces out-of-plane curvature.
Symmetric and balanced layups give B = 0 and no cure warping.
Warping also couples compressive loading into bending, lowering buckling stress.
Design rules: keep laminates symmetric and balanced, avoid excessive ply angles difference.

bank.q: Evaluate the design trade-offs in sizing a stiffened compression panel for a wing upper surface, covering skin buckling, crippling, effective width and material choice.
outline: Skin buckling sets a limit proportional to (t/b)²; thinner skin means closer stringers.
Stringers must not cripple before the panel reaches design load; check b/t of each element.
Effective width decides how much skin is counted; it falls as stress rises.
Shear lag means wide panels do not carry full bending stress across the width; note the effect on the outer stringers.
Compare aluminium with carbon fibre reinforced plastic: higher specific stiffness but brittle failure and local buckling of thin walls.
Conclude with a balanced choice and mention testing to validate crippling allowables.

glossary.def: A flat sheet whose thickness is small compared with its in-plane dimensions, so through-thickness shear is neglected.
The plane halfway through the plate thickness that is taken as the reference surface for deflection and strain.
The second derivative of deflection, ∂²w/∂x², giving how sharply the plate bends; unit 1/m.
Another name for the plate stiffness D, the plate's resistance to bending per unit curvature.
The ratio of lateral contraction to longitudinal extension under uniaxial stress; the term (1−ν²) appears in plate stiffness.
The moment carried by a unit width strip of plate, in N·m per metre of width.
The moment per unit length that twists the plate, proportional to (1−ν) times the mixed curvature.
An edge where deflection and bending moment are zero but rotation is free; idealised support in most buckling formulas.
An edge where deflection and slope are both zero, giving a higher buckling stress than a simply supported edge.
The ratio a/b of plate length to loaded width; it changes the buckling coefficient k but not the basic formula.
The extra load a buckled plate carries after the critical stress, because of membrane tension in the buckled shape.
A diagonal tensile stress pattern in a thin web after shear buckling, which lets the web carry shear well beyond the buckling load.
A longitudinal stiffening member running along the wing or fuselage that carries axial load together with the skin.
A transverse member that holds the stringers in position and keeps the cross-section shape.
Buckling of a single thin element of a section, such as one leg of an angle, while the whole column stays straight.
The width of an element measured between its corners or supported edges, used in crippling formulas.
Out-of-plane longitudinal deformation of a thin-walled section under torsion, resisted by the warping constant.
The property J of a section that measures its resistance to St Venant twisting; closed sections have far larger J than open ones.
The delay in building up bending stress in skin far from a stiffener, so the stress is not uniform across the panel width.
A single layer of composite material with one fibre direction; also called a ply.
A stack of plies bonded together with chosen fibre angles, treated as one structural plate.
A laminate whose plies are mirrored about the mid-surface, giving zero extension–bending coupling (B = 0).
A dynamic aeroelastic instability where the structure extracts energy from the airflow and vibration grows without limit.
